title: AI in PFAS Biodegradation
description: Established AI tools for biomolecular modelling fall short on PFAS because nature never evolved enzymes to train them on. A look at where AI has helped so far, why de novo enzyme design might be necessary, and what the MGB lab is exploring.
body:
AI technology is undergoing a rapid revolution, with new emergent technologies like large language models transforming the way daily work is done, and creating major results in a wide array of fields. For example, recently and quite notably a mathematics millennium problem [1] was solved by OpenAI using artificial intelligence (AI) agents. Is it possible that this powerful and novel technology could help us get closer to solving the holy grail of bioremediation, the biodegradation of poly- and perfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS)?

## Why is PFAS a problem?

PFAS is linked to various serious health problems including cancers, immunosuppression, as well as liver and kidney disease [2]. And this problem is widespread: up to approximately 70% of groundwater samples with no immediate source of contamination exceed regulatory thresholds [3].

So how come PFAS sticks around? That question is answered in more depth in [another post on this blog](https://ku-mgb.github.io/?id=why-pfas-really-persist#blog-post). The short version: the chemical attributes of PFAS make it a family of molecules highly unwilling to undergo transformation. Furthermore, there has been no evolutionary incentive for microorganisms to develop the toolkit necessary to degrade PFAS — and even if there had been, there is still the fact that the by-product of PFAS degradation, the fluoride anion, is toxic to cells.

## The research so far:

AI has been used to successfully predict the fate of PFAS in the environment, providing models for where the pollution ends up and how the molecules move in the environment [4]. Furthermore, AI has been used to predict degradation-relevant properties, allowing for differential strategies depending on the characteristics of the individual molecule [5, 6]. Examples of such differential strategies could be selecting low bond dissociation energies, a measure of the strength of a bond, for initial bioremediation efforts, to learn from the process of solving the easiest sub-problem.

However, given the AI revolution and its impact on biomolecular modelling with established tools such as AlphaFold3 [7], and emerging tools such as RFdiffusion3 [8], ESMFold2 [9], Boltz-2 [10] and more, one might think that we have all the tools needed to conduct the necessary analyses. This, however, is not so. Given the aforementioned lack of evolutionary incentive for developing enzymes capable of degrading fluorinated compounds (save a few exceptions capable of defluorinating monofluoroacetate), the training data of the previously mentioned models is incredibly sparse when it comes to enzymes that may be relevant to the breakdown of PFAS.

This is why complete *de novo* design of enzymes might be a necessity — nature simply doesn't have the needed toolkit.

## Future directions:

*De novo* enzyme design is a clear way forward to advance the field of PFAS bioremediation. But most *de novo* design methods revolve around extracting patterns in known protein data, bringing us back to the issue that the desired reaction, PFAS defluorination, does not yet have an enzyme known to be capable of it. Some models [8, 11] claim to generalise well to reactions unseen in nature, which is exactly what is needed. These models use a powerful technique from quantum chemistry called density functional theory (DFT), where the behaviour of a system can be approximated on a quantum level by considering the electron density. This trades the need for data on proteins with similar functions for intricate calculations that reveal possible active-site geometries for the desired reaction, from which the rest of the enzyme can be constructed computationally.

But these brand-new approaches have seen little use within the field of PFAS bioremediation. The closest is a preprint attempting to design PFAS-degrading enzymes using protein language models, the protein counterpart to well-known chatbot technology, which yielded inconclusive results [12].

Thus, with the advent of new technology, many potential avenues of exploration have opened up with regard to AI and PFAS bioremediation.

## AI at the MGB lab:

At the MGB lab, we are looking into state-of-the-art AI models to discover and data-mine enzymes that may degrade PFAS. This includes:

- Using the Boltz-2 model to capture structural features of enzyme–ligand pairs, to rank pairs by their likelihood of interacting.
- Using internal representations generated by protein language models to cluster enzymes by their functional homology.
- And perhaps in the future, using diffusion models to generate entirely new enzymes.
